catalog_quote: Zur Tonlehre. Slg. hat hin und wieder Starktöne bezeichnet. Ich selbst habe die musikalischen Töne festzuhalten gesucht. Wahrscheinlich sind Starktöne und musikalische Töne in der Sprache vorhanden. Die Tonhöhen scheinen sich im Satz wenig zu verändern. Klg. hat folgende Beispicle [scan; = Beispiele]: gya's gye sa re gya dok „der Kopf des Hundes ist klein". Hier hat gya's einfach Hochton, das sonst mit Hochtiefton von Klg. und mir notiert ist. Es ist denkbar, daß im Zusammenhang der Tiefton [p. 268] verloren gegangen ist; dok hat hier Tiefton, während es sonst von Klg. und mir mit Hochton gehört ist. Wahrscheinlich liegt das daran, daß das Wort hier am Satzende steht. gya's gyulik gya, gafe Klg. „der Kopf des Mannes ist groß". Hier bleibt der Hochton auch am Schluß. tốn đưlīk da dja'luž Klg. „das Maul des Löwen ist groß". Hier sind die Tonhöhen der einzelnen Worte unverändert.

new_statements.translation: On tone. Seligmann [Slg.] marked stress accents (Starktöne) here and there. I myself tried to record the musical tones [pitches]. Probably both stress accents and musical tones are present in the language. The pitches seem to change little within the sentence. Klingenheben [Klg.] has the following examples: gya's gye sa re gya dok 'the dog's head is small'. Here gya's simply has high tone, which otherwise was noted with high-falling tone by Klg. and by me. It is conceivable that in connected speech the low tone was lost; dok here has low tone, whereas otherwise Klg. and I heard it with high tone. Probably this is because the word stands at the end of the sentence here.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule. Meinhof (one speaker, 1914, plus Seligmann's and Klingenheben's notes) says the language probably has both dynamic stress ('Starktöne', marked sporadically by Seligmann with an acute) and lexical pitch (high, low, high-falling tones noted on words, changing little in sentences). Where stress falls is not described by any source opened; later sources (Schadeberg 1981 via WALS 13A; Norton & Alaki 2015; Clements & Rialland 2008) treat Jomang/Talodi as a two-level tone language and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; only sentence-final lowering of a word's high tone is remarked (dok high in isolation, low sentence-finally).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated words and a few short genitive sentences elicited from one speaker (Fatme of Jebel Talodi, El-Obeid 1914) plus Seligmann 1911 and Klingenheben wordlists; tone marks on citation forms; remark that pitches change little in the sentence.
new_statements.identity_note: Meinhof 1915-16 describes 'Talodi', the language of Jebel Talodi (speaker Fatme from the Talodi hill, plus Seligmann's 1910 Talodi list from Talodi/Tasume/Tata villages) = Glottolog talo1250 Tasomi-Tata (ISO tlo), called Jomang in Schadeberg 1981 and WALS (jom). Meinhof notes Nicholls' extra vocabulary may represent a different dialect. Not to be confused with the Talodi family/branch name, nor with talo1253 (Talossan, artificial).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog record (classification tonal; Meinhof 1915-16 'Wahrscheinlich sind Starktoene und musikalische Toene in der Sprache vorhanden', no placement) and with WALS 13A 'simple tone system' (Schadeberg 1981): Tucker & Bryan, after Stevenson, likewise report coexisting tone and dynamic stress and add that stress outweighs syllabic pitch in these groups; neither source states a stress position, so no placement rule can be entered. Caveats: group-level (Talodi-Masakin together with Koalib-Moro and Lafofa), second-hand (Stevenson 1956-57, Afrika und Uebersee 40-41, itself unread and search-only on HathiTrust), snippet-level reading with page unrecovered.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa class languages, second-hand from Stevenson 1956-57: dynamic (expiratory) stress, accompanied by high or low tone, is more important than syllabic pitch, though not equally prominent in every language of the groups; a few lexical tone doublets exist (examples given for Laro and Masakin, none for Talodi itself); the book's examples are not marked for tone or stress. Nothing is said about WHERE stress falls, and nothing specific to Talodi/Jomang: my item-restricted FTS query for 'TALODI' returned only noun-class wordlist fragments and cross-references (no stress context), and the proximity queries 'Talodi stress'~40 and 'Masakin stress'~40 inside the item returned 0 hits.
new_statements.exceptions: 'not equally prominent in all languages' (of the three groups); no language-specific exceptions
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog language is Talodi proper (Jomang, spoken on Jebel Talodi; Tasomi and Tata villages; ISO tlo; Meinhof's data from one speaker from Jebel Talodi, 1914). Tucker & Bryan's ch. 18a treats 'Talodi-Masakin (T-M)' as a group together with Koalib-Moro and Lafofa; the stress sentence is a group-level generalisation quoted from Stevenson, and the tone doublets cited are Laro (Koalib-Moro) and Masakin (= Ngile, a different Talodi-group language), so nothing in the recovered text is specific to Talodi/Jomang.
